'''''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus''''' is a [[species]] of [[moss]] known as '''springy turf-moss''' in the [[United Kingdom]],<ref name="BBS">{{cite book |editor1=Ian Atherton |editor2=Sam Bosanquet |editor3=Mark Lawley |title=Mosses and Liverworts of Britain and Ireland: A Field Guide |publisher=[[British Bryological Society]] |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-9561310-1-0 |author=Martin Godfrey |chapter=''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' |page=818 |url=http://hosting.sleath.co.uk/bbs/accounts/mosses/Rhytidiadelphus%20squarrosus_DMPT.pdf }}{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cilycwm.com/cwm_survey_lower.php |title=The lower plants of Cwm Rhaeadr Forest |author=R. G. Woods |publisher=Cilycwm.com |access-date=February 25, 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100125034358/http://www.cilycwm.com/cwm_survey_lower.php |archivedate=January 25, 2010 }}</ref> and '''square goose neck moss''' in the [[United States]].<ref name="mobot">{{cite web |url=http://www.mobot.org/plantscience/bfna/V2/HyloHylocomiaceae.htm |title=XXX. Hylocomiaceae |author=Joseph R. Rohrer  |work=Bryophyte Flora of North America, Provisional Publication |publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] |year=2008}}</ref><ref>{{ITIS |taxon=''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' |id=16384}}</ref> It is widespread in [[Eurasia]] and [[North America]], and has been introduced to the [[Southern Hemisphere]]. It has broad [[ecological tolerance]]s, and is usually found in man-made habitats such as lawns and golf courses. It is most closely related to ''[[Rhytidiadelphus subpinnatus|R. subpinnatus]]'', with which it is often confused.

==Description==
''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' grows as an extensive mat of branching stems, up to {{convert|15|cm|0}} tall,<ref name="UBC"/> sheathed in leaves that are {{convert|2|-|2.5|mm|2|abbr=on}} long and bend sharply back at a [[right angle]], and thus spread outwards from the stem.<ref name="BBS"/> The leaf bases are broad and include a pair of short nerves.<ref name="BBS"/> The plant rarely produces capsules, so most of the species' reproduction is [[asexual reproduction|asexual]].<ref name="ANBG"/>

==Distribution==
''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' has a circumpolar distribution in the [[Northern Hemisphere]],<ref name="UBC">{{cite web |url=http://www.botany.ubc.ca/bryophyte/stanleypark/rhytidiadelphus_squarrosus/index.htm |title=''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' (Hedw.) Warnst. |work=Bryophytes of Stanley Park |publisher=[[University of British Columbia]] |author=Patrick Lilley |year=2006 |access-date=February 25, 2010 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613112501/http://www.botany.ubc.ca/bryophyte/stanleypark/rhytidiadelphus_squarrosus/index.htm |archivedate=June 13, 2011 }}</ref> being found across much of Eurasia, and parts of North America, including [[British Columbia]], [[Alaska]], [[Washington (U.S. state)|Washington]], [[Oregon]], [[Newfoundland and Labrador]] and [[Greenland]].<ref name="mobot"/>

It has also been introduced to northeastern North America,<ref name="Miller"/> [[Tasmania]] and [[New Zealand]], where it is now an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://fcms.its.utas.edu.au/scieng/plantsci/project.asp?lProjectId=1955 |title=Distribution, reproductive biology and population studies of the introduced moss ''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' |publisher=[[University of Tasmania]] |access-date=February 25, 2010}}</ref> The first specimen to be collected in the [[Southern Hemisphere]] was taken in 1974 in Dundas Creek, western [[Tasmania]], but the first published record came the following year, from a [[golf course]] in [[Dunedin]] on [[New Zealand]]'s [[South Island]].<ref name="ANBG">{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/bryophyte/bryogeography-imports-exports.html |title=Bryogeography: imports and exports |work=Australian Bryophytes |publisher=[[Australian National Botanic Gardens]], [[Australian National Herbarium]] |access-date=February 25, 2010}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Rhytidiadelphus.squarrosus.jpg|thumb|left|''R. squarrosus'' growing in the [[Belgium|Belgian]] [[Ardennes]]]]
It tolerates a wide variety of soil conditions, from [[calcareous grassland]] to [[Heath (habitat)|acid heaths]]. It grows most conspicuously in heavily grazed [[pasture]]s and on the regularly mown [[Fairway (golf)|fairways]] on golf courses,<ref name="ANBG"/> and is the most common moss found in [[lawn]]s in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://home.clara.net/adhale/bryos/rloreus.htm |title=''Rhytidiadelphus loreus'' |work=Mosses and liverworts in Wales |author=Alan Hale |access-date=February 25, 2010 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080407190151/http://home.clara.net/adhale/bryos/rloreus.htm |archivedate=April 7, 2008}}</ref> It is almost always found in association with humans, leaving its original habitat unclear; it may have evolved as a plant of coastal [[meadow]]s.<ref name="Miller">{{cite journal |journal=[[Rhodora (journal)|Rhodora]] |volume=111 |issue=946 |pages=218–230 |year=2009 |doi=10.3119/08-7.1 |title=Mosses adventive and naturalized in the northeastern United States: new examples and new distributional records |author=Norton G. Miller}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' was formally named (as ''Hypnum squarrosum'') by [[Johann Hedwig]] in his 1801 work ''[[Species Muscorum]]'',<ref name="mobot"/> which is considered the starting point for the [[botanical nomenclature|nomenclature]] of most mosses.<ref>{{cite book |title=International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (Vienna Code) |editor1=J. McNeill |editor2=F. R. Barrie |editor3=H. M. Burdet |year=2006 |series=Regnum Vegetabile 146 |publisher=Gantner Verlag KG |isbn=3-906166-48-1 |url=http://ibot.sav.sk/icbn/main.htm|display-editors=etal}}</ref>

Although ''R. squarrosus'' and ''R. subpinnatus'' have sometimes been considered varieties of a single species, particularly by botanists from the United States,<ref name="mobot"/> studies using [[Microsatellite (genetics)|microsatellites]] show them to be separate.<ref name="Korpelainen">{{cite journal |journal=[[Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution]] |volume=48 |issue=1 |year=2008 |pages=372–376 |doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2008.04.007 |title=Molecular evidence shows that the moss ''Rhytidiadelphus subpinnatus'' (Hylocomiaceae) is clearly distinct from ''R. squarrosus'' |author=H. Korpelainen |author2=V. Virtanen |author3=K. Kostamo |author4=H. Karttunen |name-list-style=amp |pmid=18501641|bibcode=2008MolPE..48..372K }}</ref> The two are often confused, however, and reports of ''R. squarrosus'' may sometimes refer to ''R. subpinnatus''.<ref name="Miller"/> Indeed, both ''R. subpinnatus'' and ''[[Rhytidiadelphus japonicus|R. japonicus]]'' were originally described as [[Infraspecific taxon|infraspecific taxa]] within ''R. squarrosus''.<ref name="mobot"/>

In contrast to ''R. triquetrus'' and ''[[Rhytidiadelphus loreus|R. loreus]]'', ''R. squarrosus'', ''R. subpinnatus'' and ''R. japonicus'' have leaves which are not pleated. ''R. squarrosus'' differs from ''R. japonicus'' in having a long point at the leaf tips, and from ''R. subpinnatus'' in the closer spacing of the leaves on the stem, such that the stem can only be seen through the bases of the leaves; in ''R. subpinnatus'', parts of the stem are visible directly.<ref name="mobot"/>

A new genus, ''[[Rhytidiastrum]]'', has been proposed for a group of species including ''R. squarrosus'' and ''R. subpinnatus'', but not ''[[Rhytidiadelphus triquetrus|R. triquetrus]]''.<ref name="mobot"/>

==Response to herbicide application==
In a study of the effect of the herbicide [[Asulam]] on moss growth, ''Rhytidiadelphus squarrosus'' was shown to have intermediate [[sensitivity (physiology)|sensitivity]] to Asulam exposure.<ref name="Rowntree 2003">{{cite journal | title=Exposure to Asulox Inhibits the Growth of Mosses | journal=Annals of Botany |date= 2003 | volume=92 | issue= 4 | pages=547–556 | first1=J. K. | last1=Rowntree | first2=K. F. | last2=Lawton |first3=F. J. | last3=Rumsey | first4=E. | last4=Sheffield| doi=10.1093/aob/mcg166 | pmid=12933364 | pmc=4243670 | url=https://doi.org/10.1093/aob/mcg166 }}</ref>

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Rhytidiadelphus'' derives from the words ''Rhytidium'' and {{lang|el|[[:wikt:ἀδελφός|ἀδελφός]]}} (''adelfós'', [[brother]]), implying a close relationship to the genus ''[[Rhytidium]]''.<ref name="mobot"/> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''squarrosus'' refers to the leaves, which are [[:wikt:squarrose|squarrose]], having a right-angled bend which causes the tips to extend away from the stem.<ref name="mobot"/>
